# Family and Relationships

### Life Stages
| Spanish | English | Example Sentence | Notes |

| nacer | to be born | Nací en mil novecientos noventa y cinco. | Irregular preterite: nací, naciste, nació... Use preterite (single event). |

| casarse | to get married | Se casaron en junio. | Reflexive. **Casarse con** alguien (marry someone) — NOT "casarse a." |
| divorciarse | to get divorced | | Reflexive. **Divorciarse de** alguien. |
| morir | to die | | Irregular preterite: murió, murieron (o→u stem change). Standard/neutral. |
| fallecer | to pass away | Mi abuelo falleció el año pasado. | Formal/euphemistic. Preferred when speaking respectfully about someone's death. |

## Common Collocations
- **llevarse bien/mal con** — to get along well/badly with; always reflexive, always with **con**
- **parecerse a** — to look like / resemble; always reflexive, always with **a**
- **casarse con** — to marry someone; NOT "casarse a." "Se casó con María."
- **estar embarazada** — to be pregnant; uses **estar** (temporary state)
- **ser hijo/a único/a** — to be an only child
- **familia numerosa** — large family; set phrase
- **de niño/a** — as a child; imperfect trigger ("De niño, yo vivía en...")
- **cuando era joven** — when I was young; classic imperfect context
- **tener... años** — to be... years old; uses **tener**, not **ser** or **estar**

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **embarazada** vs **embarrassed**: **Embarazada** means "pregnant." This is one of the most famous false cognates in Spanish. Embarrassed = **avergonzado/a**. "Estoy embarazada" does NOT mean "I'm embarrassed."
- **parientes** vs **parents**: **Parientes** means "relatives." Parents = **padres**. "Mis parientes" = my relatives, NOT my parents.
- **realizar** vs **realize**: **Realizar** means "to carry out / accomplish." To realize (become aware) = **darse cuenta de**. "Me di cuenta de que..." = "I realized that..."
- **querer** vs **amar**: Both mean "to love," but **querer** is the everyday word for loving family and partners. **Amar** is stronger, more literary or passionate. "Te quiero" is the standard way to say "I love you" to family and partners. "Te amo" is reserved for deep romantic love.
- **mayor** vs **viejo**: For family age comparisons, always use **mayor** (Mi hermano mayor). Using **viejo** for people sounds disrespectful unless used affectionately as slang ("mi viejo" = my old man/dad in some countries).

## Dialect Variations
- **to miss someone**: **extrañar** (Latin America), **echar de menos** (Spain). Both are universally understood.
- **husband**: **esposo** (formal/universal), **marido** (common everyday), **mi viejo** (Argentina, very informal/affectionate)
- **wife**: **esposa** (formal/universal), **mujer** (common everyday, literally "woman" — not considered reductive in this context), **mi vieja** (Argentina, very informal/affectionate)
- **kids (informal)**: **niños** (universal), **chamacos** (Mexico, informal), **chicos** (Argentina), **nenes** (Caribbean)
- **buddy/dude (used like family)**: **güey/wey** (Mexico), **tío/tía** (Spain), **che** (Argentina), **pana** (Venezuela/Caribbean)
- **dad/mom (informal)**: **papá/mamá** (universal), **papi/mami** (Caribbean, affectionate — also used between couples), **jefe/jefa** (Mexico, slang for parent)

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Extended family closeness**: In most of Latin America, extended family (abuelos, tíos, primos) plays a central role in daily life. Regular Sunday family gatherings are common. "¿Cómo está tu familia?" is a genuine question, not small talk.
- **La quinceañera**: A girl's 15th birthday celebration, marking the transition to womanhood. Major event in Mexico, Central America, and parts of South America. Involves a formal party, waltz, church ceremony. The celebrant is also called **la quinceañera**.
- **Naming conventions**: Many Spanish-speaking people carry two surnames — the father's first, then the mother's. "María López García" — López is from her father, García from her mother. This is standard, not a sign of a hyphenated name.
- **Godparents (padrinos)**: The **padrino** and **madrina** have a genuine social role. The relationship between parents and godparents (**compadre/comadre**) creates a bond between families. "Mi compadre" is a term of deep respect and affection.
- **Imperfect for childhood memories**: This cluster naturally pairs with the imperfect tense. "De niño, vivía con mis abuelos" (As a child, I lived with my grandparents). "Mi abuela siempre cocinaba tamales" (My grandmother always made tamales). Descriptions and habitual actions in the past = imperfect.
- **Preterite for life events**: Single, completed life events use preterite. "Nací en..." (I was born in...), "Mis padres se casaron en..." (My parents got married in...), "Mi abuelo falleció..." (My grandfather passed away...).

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **abuelo** — the **ue** is a diphthong: a-BWE-lo. Do not separate into a-bu-e-lo.
- **cuñado** — the **ñ** is its own sound, not "n+y": cu-ÑA-do.
- **pareja** — the **j** is Spanish /x/ (guttural h): pa-RE-ja.
- **quinceañera** — five syllables: kin-se-a-ÑE-ra. The **ñ** is critical.
- **fallecer** — stress on second syllable: fa-ye-SER (with Latin American yeísmo for **ll**).
- **suegra** — the **ue** is a diphthong: SWE-gra. One syllable for "sue."
